text:
Newmarket Registry
No. 20211/04

DATE:   2007·IV·23

CITATION:
Attar (Amos) v.
Attar

SUPERIOR  COURT  OF  JUSTICE

FAMILY  COURT

BETWEEN:

ELISE  ATTAR  (AMOS),

Applicant,

—  AND  —

JOE  ATTAR,

Respondent.

Before Justice Thomas M. Wood

Heard on 13 and 16-20
April 2007

Reasons for
Judgment released on 23 April 2007

CUSTODY OF CHILD — Best interests of child —
Love, affection and emotional ties — In course of litigation, which custodial
mother regarded as contest over control of children, she engaged in
mean-spirited conduct (such as hiring private investigator, her attempts to
break up father’s new relationship and slanderous statements made about him to
Office of Children’s Lawyer) — She had become absorbed by hatred of and
resentment towards father, which clouded her judgment with respect to children,
attempting to poison their minds against their father and his family — Evidence
of Children’s Lawyer was that mother’s relationship with children was somewhat
distant, compared with that of father — It was to father to whom children look
first for affection — For this and other reasons, court chose father’s home as
children’s principal residence in joint custody regime.

CUSTODY OF CHILD — Best interests of child —
Provision of guidance, education and necessaries of life — Home of custodial
mother was more chaotic for children (8, 7 and 5 years old) partly because she
was single parent but also because she was so preoccupied and consumed by
litigation that she became distant from children — As result of their various
special needs, children required great deal of attention and extensive help
with homework and school projects, which father’s home with its disciplinary
measures was able to provide — Particularly youngest child, whose disabilities
presented special challenge, had limitations that mother had difficulty in
accepting — Unfortunately, at mother’s home, children spent more time in front
of television while she preoccupied herself in other matters or on computer —
For this and other reasons, court chose father’s home as children’s principal
residence in joint custody regime.

CUSTODY OF CHILD — Mobility rights — Grounds
for allowing or denying move — General — Court reviewed and applied 7 factors
listed in
Gordon
v. Goertz
,
1996 CanLII 191 (SCC)
, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27 to facts of this case to conclude that it was
not
in best interest of children (8, 7 and 5
years old, who had lived in Thornhill, north of Toronto, all their lives) to
move to Montréal with their mother.

STATUTES AND REGULATIONS CITED

Children’s
Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-12 [as
amended], subsection
24(2).

Divorce Act
, R.S.C. 1985 (2nd Supp.), c. 3 [as amended], section 16 and subsection 16(8).

Marriage
Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. M‑3 [as amended], section
31

CASES CITED

Gordon
v. Goertz
, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27, 196 N.R. 321, 141 Sask. R. 241, [1996] 5
W.W.R. 457, 114 W.A.C. 241, 134 D.L.R. (4th) 321, 19 R.F.L. (4th) 177, [1996]
R.D.F. 209,
1996
CanLII 191
, [1996] S.C.J. No. 52, 1996 Cars­well­Sask 199.

Albert Diniz  ...........................................................................................................   for
the applicant

Heather A. McGee  ..............................................................................................   for
the respondent

Helen Trentos  ...........   for the
Office of the Children’s Lawyer, legal representative for the children

[
1
]

JUSTICE T.M. WOOD:—  Elise Amos and Joe
Attar were married on 11 January1998.  They separated in August 2004.  This
application was commenced on 6 December 2004 almost two and a half years ago.  It
has produced two banker’s boxes worth of paper.  Legal fees have consumed all
of the family’s modest assets and left each heavily indebted to former counsel.
Not one issue — even the fact of their marriage — has been settled.  They have
not been well served by the legal system nor have they used it wisely.

[
2
]

By agreement of the parties’ present counsel,
the trial has been bifurcated.  They have led evidence only with respect to the
issues of custody and access.  As requested, I am providing a ruling and
reasons on those issues before the financial issues are litigated.  Counsel for
the respondent has stipulated that I may assume a regular and dependable source
of income for the respondent of between $65,000 and $70,000 for support
purposes in making my findings on the custody and access issues.

1:     BACKGROUND

[
3
]

The parties met in the summer of 1997.  Both
come from traditional Jewish families who describe themselves as observant,
although not ultra orthodox.  The marriage was arranged.  The parties saw very
little of each other prior to their marriage in January 1998.  Each wished to
lead evidence that I discouraged on the issue of whether or not the marriage
should be annulled as the respondent’s decree absolute of divorce did not issue
until after the wedding date.  I am satisfied that each believed that they were
going through a valid ceremony of marriage.  Therefore, section
31 (marriages solemnized in good faith) of the
Marriage
Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. M-3, as amended, operates to validate their
union.  Nothing turns on this issue as they are both entitled to a divorce on
the grounds of separation and both wish this to occur.

[
4
]

The parties had three children in rapid
succession.  David the eldest was born on 7 October 1998.  He is now eight.
Sarah was born the following year on 9 September 1999.  She is now seven.
Daniel was born two years later on 4 September 2001.  He is now five.

[
5
]

The children were very young while the
parties were together.  During this period, the applicant was their primary
caregiver.  The respondent has always worked outside the home as an electronics
technician.  The applicant worked from home in a business run by her and her
father, supplying Japanese animated videos and DVDs.  This gave her the ability
to arrange her hours of work around the needs of the children.  The family
employed a nanny for some time before separation.

[
6
]

The respondent indicated that he felt the
parties were good parents working as a team while together.  The applicant was
excellent at seeing to the children’s physical needs and ensuring that they
were always well turned out and organized.  The respondent felt that he was the
warmer of the two parties and provided the children with affection and companionship
that they would not otherwise have received.

[
7
]

It is not clear what precipitated the
separation.  However, it is not difficult to imagine the difficulties this
young couple would have encountered marrying when they did not yet know each
other well and having three children within the space of as many years.  Each
was holding down a full-time job and they had taken on a large house and heavy
expenses.

[
8
]

Whatever the reason may have been, it was
the applicant who requested a divorce during the fall of 2003.  The respondent
attempted marriage counselling but to no avail.  The parties endured eight
unpleasant months under the same roof before the respondent moved to his
parent’s home at the request of the applicant.

[
9
]

After separation, each party acted towards
the other with a petty vindictiveness that does neither of them credit.  The
respondent used his computer skills to disrupt the applicant’s business.  He
has also attempted to portray that business as one dealing extensively in
pornographic material.  The applicant denied the respondent contact with the
children, had him spied upon and hacked into his computer procuring highly
personal and compromising evidence of his use of computer dating services.  She
has also attempted to sabotage his new relationship.

[
10
]

The applicant and the children remained in
the former matrimonial home.  The respondent resided with his parents.
Although the applicant indicates that the respondent’s access was sporadic for
the first few months of separation, I am satisfied that this was as much her
fault as his.  Access and child support were settled by consent order dated 18 February
2005.  The access arrangement that continues to this day provided for the respondent
to have the children every second week from after school on Thursday until the
following Monday morning, plus Wednesday night overnight on the week not
followed by a weekend access period.

[
11
]

Each party gave lengthy evidence about
difficulties with this access regime.  These centered on pick up and drop off.
Since the respondent worked full time, he had his parents pick up the children
after school.  The applicant objected to this and attempted to obtain evidence
through a private investigator that the respondent was leaving the children
with his parents for most of the access visits.  It is significant that this
investigator was unsuccessful in establishing that this was the case.  The
applicant also made much of the fact that the respondent drives a somewhat
unsuitable car with a nominal backseat.  It is clear that, for some time, the
respondent did not have proper child safety seats in the car although, with a
push from York Regional Police, that has now been remedied.

[
12
]

In March 2006, the applicant suddenly left
for Montréal where she remained for 17 days leaving the children with the
respondent.  Her stated reason for going was that the respondent had ceased to
pay his share of the mortgage payments as ordered.  As a result, she had to be
in Montréal where the business was headquartered, to assist her father.  This
was apparently a condition precedent to her obtaining an advance from him.

[
13
]

The respondent is unclear why the applicant
went to Montréal without warning to him.  He indicates that he was forced to
rely on Jewish Family and Children’s Services for clothing for the children as
she left them without adequate supplies for that time of year.  He has made
much of this to support his argument that the applicant does not care for the
children or their feelings.  It would appear likely that the applicant was
overwhelmed by the intensity of the litigation, the attempt to cope with three
children by herself and with what she perceived to be the respondent’s lack of
co-operation, and may have had a temporary breakdown.  Whatever the reason, she
returned after 17 days and the prior access arrangement resumed.

[
14
]

The respondent, who maintained an Internet
dating profile on one or more sites as Joe Cool, met Denise March online in
late December 2005 or January 2006.  They began dating in January.  The
respondent carefully and responsibly introduced her to the children beginning
in March.  They leased a home together at the end of June.  It is clear from
the evidence of the respondent, his mother, the children’s lawyer, and Ms.
March herself, that she plays a significant role in the care of the children
when they are with their father.  She is committed to the children and to their
care.  The respondent describes her as a stabilizing influence on his life and
I wholeheartedly agree with him on this point.

[
15
]

At the present time, the elder children
attend Wilshire Public School,
which is located in the catchment area of the former matrimonial home.  Daniel
attends Loving Care Daycare, a facility catering to Jewish families that
provides day care, junior and senior kindergarten and some component of Hebrew
training.  All three children attended at this facility up to the end of junior
kindergarten.  There is presently some tension between the parties over
Daniel’s schooling, as the respondent would like him to attend the same school
as his siblings.  His reasons are that there would be no fees at the public
school and he believes that it provides a more rigorous academic program.  The
applicant on the other hand, believes that Daniel should complete senior
kindergarten in his present location.

[
16
]

Each of the children poses challenges.
David has been identified as learning-disabled.  He spends half of each day in
a special classroom with a one-on-one teacher.  He has an extremely short attention
span and requires intensive supervision with homework or projects of any kind.  Sarah
also struggles somewhat with her schoolwork, although she is not as challenged
as David.  Although friendly and outgoing, she is somewhat needy and prone to
outbursts of temper.  Daniel poses behavioural difficulties and suffers from
enuresis.  He is aggressive with his brother and behaves inappropriately with
adults to obtain attention.

[
17
]

The applicant hopes to move with the
children to Montréal where her family resides.  She has free accommodation
there in a duplex owned by her parents.  She also feels that her chances of
obtaining employment there would be much better than here as her extended family
have extensive business contacts.  She wishes the children to attend private
Jewish schools.  It is her belief that the fees for this type of establishment
are far lower in the province of Québec.

[
18
]

The respondent wishes the children to remain
in Ontario.  He believes that
Wilshire is an excellent school.  90% of its enrolment is Jewish and it makes
some allowance for this in its curriculum, providing some Hebrew and Jewish
history on a regular basis.  He feels that the applicant has skills, which
would allow her to obtain employment in Ontario and she should try to do so.  He points out the difficulties of
maintaining contact between his side of the family and the children were the
applicant to move them to Montréal.

2:     DISCUSSION

2.1:     The Parties

[
19
]

Before turning to the specific issues raised
by this case, I wish to note that I have serious reservations about both
parties as parents.  The applicant is a very bitter person.  While such a
reaction may be understandable in the face of the destruction of her marriage,
the depth of her antagonism towards the respondent and its continued intensity
three and a quarter years after the separation cause me grave concern.

[
20
]

She has hired a private detective to follow
the respondent and Ms. Marsh in an attempt to discredit them.  That
investigator presumably on her instructions entered into an unseemly
contretemps with the York Regional Police in an attempt to have the respondent
charged with a series of infractions that could have led to the loss of his
driving privileges.

[
21
]

She hacked into the respondent’s computer
and filed his immature and untruthful dating profiles in evidence.  She has
continued to monitor the sites to obtain evidence that this activity continues
notwithstanding his relationship with Ms. Marsh.  She attempted to enlist the
aid of the Children’s Lawyer in obtaining evidence against him, which had
nothing to do with the children.  She also falsely accused him of having a
sexually transmitted disease, making this allegation in a way calculated to
ensure that it would sow doubt in Ms. March’s mind about her partner.

[
22
]

Her evidence and the conduct of her case
were so focused on the respondent that I had difficulty believing her oft
repeated mantra — that what she was doing was in the best interest of the
children.

[
23
]

The respondent has a lot of growing up to
do.  The applicant’s internet sleuthing has established that he maintains the
Joe Cool profile on at least one site and is still occasionally active on it.  This
is not only stupid, but also untruthful, if he is as committed to his new
relationship as he says he is.

[
24
]

He also continues to drive a two-door sports
coupe with what can best be described as a nominal back seat.  Such a vehicle
is both uncomfortable and unsuitable for transporting the children to whom he
professes such a commitment.  He confesses that Ms. March does the cooking and
laundry while he concentrates on the children.  This is no doubt nice for him
but hardly a fair division of labour.  It is high time that he traded in “Joe
Cool” for “Mr. Dad”.

2.2:     Mobility

[
25
]

The applicant’s position that it is in the
best interest of the children to move with her to Montreal means that this is a classic “mobility case”.  As such, it should
be decided in accordance with the guidelines set down by the Supreme Court of
Canada in the well-known decision of
Gordon
v. Goertz
.
[1]

The procedure to be followed is summarized in paragraphs [49] and [50] of the
majority decision delivered by Justice Beverley McLachlin (as she then was):

[49]
The
law can be summarized as follows:

1.

The parent applying for a change in the
custody or access order must meet the threshold requirement of demonstrating
a material change in the circumstances affecting the child.

2.

If the threshold is met, the judge on the
application must embark on a fresh inquiry into what is in the best interests
of the child, having regard to all the relevant circumstances relating to the
child’s needs and the ability of the respective parents to satisfy them.

3.

This inquiry is based on the findings of
the judge who made the previous order and evidence of the new circumstances.

4.

The inquiry does not begin with a legal presumption
in favour of the custodial parent, although the custodial parent’s views are
entitled to great respect.

5.

Each case turns on its own unique
circumstances.  The only issue is the best interest of the child in the
particular circumstances of the case.

6.

The focus is on the best interests of the
child, not the interests and rights of the parents.

7.

More particularly the judge should
consider,
inter alia
:

(a)

the existing custody arrangement and
relationship between the child and the custodial parent;

(b)

the existing access arrangement and the
relationship between the child and the access parent;

(c)

the desirability of maximizing contact
between the child and both parents;

(d)

the view of the child;

(e)

the custodial parent’s reason for moving,
only in the exceptional case where it is relevant to that parent’s ability to
meet the needs of the child;

(f)

disruption to the child of a change in
custody;

(g)

disruption to the child consequent on
removal from family, schools, and the community he or she has come to know.

[50]
In
the end, the importance of the child’s remaining with the parent to whose custody
it has become accustomed in the new location must be weighed against the
continuance of full contact with the child’s access parent, its extended
family and its community.  The ultimate question in every case is this:  what
is in the best interests of the child in all the circumstances, old as well
as new?

[
26
]

Applying the criteria set out above to the
facts of this case, I make the following findings.

[
27
]

The first part of the two-part test does not
apply in this case, as there is no final order with respect to custody and
access.

2.2(a):     The Existing Custody Arrangement and Relationship
between the Child and the Custodial Parent

[
28
]

The applicant has been the primary caregiver
of the children through most of their lives.  They have always lived with her
and she has done most, though not all, of the myriad tasks required of a
parent.  The children have a strong bond with her and know they can look to her
to satisfy their material needs.  That said, however, there is some clear
evidence of conflict between the children and their mother, which may increase
as they get older.  There is also evidence that their relationship with her is
not as warm and comfortable as it might be with another less driven and less
bitter parent.

2.2(b):     The Existing Access Arrangement and the Relationship
between the Child and the Access Parent

[
29
]

The children’s relationship with the
respondent has grown stronger in the years since separation.  When the parties
were together, he was a somewhat secondary figure.  This was partly because
they were very young and he worked outside the home, and partly because he
remained somewhat immature and unwilling to accept the responsibilities of parenthood.
That said, I am satisfied that he was always an important person in their
lives.  He provided a warmth and spontaneity that would not otherwise have been
available to them.

[
30
]

Immediately following separation, the
respondent, by his own admission, had some difficulty accepting his role in the
children’s lives as a single parent during access periods.  However, in the
last two years and particularly, since his relationship with Ms. Marsh, his
life has stabilized and the children have become his primary focus.  The
evidence of the Children’s Lawyer is that he has become extremely important to
the children and that their relationship with him is a stronger and less
problematic one than their relationship with their mother.

2.2(c):     The Desirability of Maximizing Contact between
the Child and Both Parents

[
31
]

Although the applicant bravely plans to
drive the children back and forth between Toronto and Montréal every second weekend for much of the year, this will
not, and should not happen.  Such a drive at that frequency would exhaust both
the applicant and the children.  It would cause them to miss an unacceptable
amount of school and, as the respondent correctly surmised, it would alienate
the children from him.  As such, it is not in the best interests of the
children.  The reality of a move to Montréal will be that the children are cut
off from contact with their father except during longer holidays and by means
of the telephone or Internet.

[
32
]

The evidence before me is that this would
not be in their best interest.  The children clearly derive great benefit from
their frequent and intimate contact with their father.  He is the one
responsible for their leisure activities and his interaction with them is vital
to their well-being.

2.2(d):     The Views of the Child

[
33
]

The Children’s Lawyer’s instructions from
the elder two children are that they wish to spend equal amounts of time with
each parent.  Daniel would like to see more of his father.

2.2(e):     The Custodial Parent’s Reason for Moving, Only
in the Exceptional Case Where It Is Relevant to That Parent’s Ability to Meet
the Needs of the Child

[
34
]

The applicant has testified that her move to
Montréal has a direct bearing upon her ability to provide for the children.
She paints the respondent as unwilling to assume his financial responsibility
either for the children or for herself.  She stopped working in the business
run by her and her father in August 2006 when she says it was shut down.  She
has been relying solely upon child support and gifts from her father since that
time.

[
35
]

She and her father have testified that a
duplex in his building is available to her free of charge should she move.  They
have also indicated that, although she has no clear plans for employment, her
father would be prepared to provide for her if she wished to retrain or to make
use of his extensive network of contacts and relatives in Montréal to find her
employment.

[
36
]

The respondent has paid child support since
he was ordered to do so in February 2005.  His lawyer has stipulated that he
has a stable income of $65,000-$70,000 available to pay child support and, if
necessary, spousal support.  Although the bifurcated nature of the trial has
prevented me from hearing evidence of the applicant’s ability to earn an income,
it is apparent from what little has been led, that the applicant contributed
significantly to the family finances while operating the business with her
father.

[
37
]

Lack of evidence prevents me from making a
determinative finding in this area.  However, it appears that, while life would
be easier in Montréal for the applicant, it is by no means certain that she
would be unable to provide adequately for herself and the children with
assistance from the respondent, in Toronto.

2.2(f):      Disruption to the Child of a Change in Custody

[
38
]

Each party to this action seeks sole
custody.  The parties have now been separated almost 3 years and a
status
quo
has developed in which the children see each parent overnight regularly
each week.  Each parent does activities with the children.  The presence of
each parent is a regular factor in the children’s lives.  Were the children
either to move with their mother to Montréal or to remain here with their
father while their mother moved alone, their loss would be significant.

2.2(g):     Disruption to the Child Consequent on Removal
from Family, Schools and the Community He or She Has Come to Know

[
39
]

The children have lived north of Toronto in Thornhill all their lives.
Almost all of the respondent’s family resides in this area.  The children are
old enough that they have school friends and neighbourhood friends.  Their
synagogue is in this area.  All of this would be lost were they to move to
Montréal.

[
40
]

It will be clear from a review of the
findings set out above that it is not in the children’s best interest that they
move to Montréal.  They should remain in this area.  That being the case, the
issue now becomes which custody and residency structure is in their best interest.

3:     CUSTODY

[
41
]

Since the applicant has claimed a divorce,
custody is determined in accordance with the provisions of
section 16
of the
Divorce Act
,
R.S.C. 1985 (2nd Supp.), c. 3, as amended.  Subsection 16(8) provides:

(8)
Factors.—
In
making an order under this section, the court shall take into consideration
only the best interests of the child of the marriage as determined by reference
to the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the child.

[
42
]

The best interests test set out in section 16 has been
adopted in more recent Ontario
legislation dealing with custody and access, the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-12, as amended.

[
43
]

Subsection
24(2) of the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
provides a useful codification of much of the case law
in the area in the form of a checklist of factors to be taken into consideration
when determining best interests.  It directs the court to consider all the
needs and circumstances of the child including seven enumerated factors.

[
44
]

When determining questions of custody and
access under
section 16

of the
Divorce Act
,
it is useful to refer to this checklist, as it is a fuller and more
comprehensive guide than that provided in the earlier legislation. Its headings
are as follows:

(
a
)

the love, affection and emotional ties
between the child and,

(i)

each person entitled to or claiming
custody of or access to the child,

(ii)

other members of the child’s family who
reside with the child, and

(iii)

persons involved in the care and
upbringing of the child;

(
b
)

the views and preferences of the child,
where such views and preferences can reasonably be ascertained;

(
c
)

the length of time the child has lived in
a stable home environment;

(
d
)

the ability and willingness of each
person applying for custody of the child to provide the child with guidance
and education, the necessaries of life and any special needs of the child;

(
e
)

any plans proposed for the care and
upbringing of the child;

(
f
)

the permanence and stability of the
family unit with which it is proposed that the child will live; and

(
g
)

the relationship by blood or through an
adoption order between the child and each person who is a party to the
application.

[
45
]

Applying these criteria to the facts of this
case, I make the following findings.

3.1:     The Love, Affection and Emotional Ties between
the Child and Each Party and His or Her Family

[
46
]

The Attar children are extremely lucky in
having two parents each with extended family, to love and support them.
Although the applicant is on her own in Ontario, she is supported both financially and emotionally by her parents
in Montréal.  She travels there frequently with the children who have a close
relationship with their cousins in Québec.

[
47
]

The respondent is very close to his parents
both physically and emotionally.  His father picks up the children at the
beginning of each access period.  They spend time at their grandparents before
going to their father’s house with their parents.  They regularly spend the
Sabbath with their father and Ms. March at the respondent’s parents’ home.
There is extensive extended family in this area.

[
48
]

While a review of the maternal and paternal
extended families would appear to be more or less even, the children’s relationships
with their parents do not fall into the same category.  Unfortunately the only
conclusion that can be drawn from the evidence looked at as a whole, is that
the applicant continues to be consumed by hatred of and resentment towards the
respondent.  Her life has focused to a large extent on what she perceives to be
a contest between them over control of the children.  Only such an attitude can
explain the mean-spirited actions she has taken during the course of this litigation,
including the work of the private investigator, her attempts to break up the
respondent’s new relationship and the slanderous statements made about the
respondent in the material filed with the Children’s Lawyer.  These emotions
have clouded her judgment with respect to the children.  She has clearly
attempted to poison their minds against their father and his family, but
thankfully has been unsuccessful in doing so.

[
49
]

The evidence of the Children’s Lawyer is
that the applicant’s relationship with the children is somewhat distant
compared with that of their father.  It is to the respondent that the children
look first for affection.

[
50
]

The respondent although slow to take on the
responsibilities of parenthood, has now shouldered them and is showing
increasing commitment.  His new relationship has withstood the pressure of
three troubled children and the applicant’s attempts to sabotage it.  His new
partner, Ms. Marsh, has fully accepted the children and earned a place in their
hearts as an important caregiver.

3.2:     The Child’s Views and Preferences

[
51
]

The children expressed differing views and
preferences throughout the course of the Children’s Lawyer’s investigation.  However,
since October, the elder two have been consistent in their wish to see each of
their parents an equal amount of the time.  Daniel wishes to spend more time
with his father.

3.3:     The Length of Time the Child Has Lived in a Stable
Home Environment

[
52
]

The children have always resided with their
mother.  From the date of separation until the early fall of 2006, this was in
the former matrimonial home.  Since that time, it has been in rented
accommodation in the same municipality.  Since separation, the children have
visited with their father.  Initially, this was at the home of his parents,
then in an apartment and, since June 2006, in a rented home with their father
and Ms. Marsh.

[
53
]

Since 2005, they have followed an access
regime that has them in their father’s home for a four-day weekend once every
two weeks and an overnight in the middle of the off week.  The evidence of the
Children’s Lawyer is that, although they have their own rooms and possessions
in each location, the more stable routine is in the home of the respondent.  This
is thanks in no small measure to the efforts of Ms. Marsh.  Thus, to the extent
that any shared parenting regime fraught with the animosity of this one can be
stable; this is the arrangement to which the children are used.

3.4:     The Ability and Willingness of Each Party to Provide
Guidance, Education, the Necessities of Life, and to Care for Any Special Needs
of the Child

[
54
]

This is the crucial factor in this case.  I
have already alluded to some of the concerns surrounding the care given to the
children by the applicant.  The evidence of the Children’s Lawyer is that life
is more chaotic for the children in the applicant’s home.  This stems only in
part from the fact that she is a single parent.  It is equally due to the fact
that she is preoccupied and consumed with this litigation and, as a result,
distant from the children.

[
55
]

All three children need a great deal of
attention.  Ms. Marsh’s presence in the respondent’s household allows him to
provide that attention.  It appears that he is willing and able to do so.  The
children’s behaviour in the respondent’s home appears to be better than in the
home of the applicant.  The disciplinary measures taken when they do get out of
line appear to be more consistent in his household as well.

[
56
]

David and Sarah both need extensive help
with homework and school projects.  This occurs in the home of the respondent
on a regular basis.  Unfortunately, this is not the case in the home of the
applicant.  The children spend more time there in front of the television set
because the applicant is preoccupied or on the computer.

[
57
]

David’s learning disabilities provide a
special challenge.  He is a handful because of his inability to focus on any
task for more than a few minutes at a time.  In the respondent’s household, it
is not only the respondent but also Ms. Marsh and the respondent’s mother who
are ready and able to work consistently with David.  The applicant is both less
inclined and less able to do so.  She is less inclined because she has
difficulty in accepting David’s limitations.  She is less able to do so because
she does not have the assistance that the respondent has.

3.5:     The Parties’ Plans for the Child’s Care and Upbringing

[
58
]

The applicant’s plan was to move the
children to Montréal where she has an extensive support system.  The
respondent’s plan is that the children would live with him and visit with the
applicant in a reversal of the present access.

[
59
]

For the reasons set out above, it is my
conclusion that a move to Montreal is not in the children’s best interests.  The applicant’s backup
plan is somewhat unclear, although she has expressed willingness through counsel,
to remain in this area and continue the present access regime.  Assuming that
the applicant’s plan is to remain in Thornhill, each plan could be
characterized as a continuation of the
status quo
.  As I have indicated,
that
status quo
favours the home of the respondent over that of the
applicant as the primary residence of the children.

3.6:     The Permanence and Stability of Each Family Unit

[
60
]

As indicated immediately above, the
permanence and stability of the applicant’s household is unclear at present.
She has no employment.  She is dependent upon child support from the respondent
and gifts from her father on an
ad hoc
basis.  Her previous business,
although apparently quite successful, has been closed down.  It is unclear
whether it could be restarted or, if it were, how profitable it would be.

[
61
]

The applicant has testified that, if she
were to remain in Thornhill, she would need assistance from the respondent.
While he makes a reasonable income, it is certainly not enough to maintain the
two households at their present level without considerable contribution from
the applicant.

[
62
]

The respondent’s relationship with Ms. March
is now 16 months old.  They have lived together for nine months.  The evidence
of the respondent, Ms. March, and the respondent’s mother is consistent.  The
relationship is a strong one and the respondent and Ms. March are committed to
a long-term partnership.

[
63
]

While it is early days yet, the fact that
the relationship has withstood the mischievous acts of the applicant and the
pressures imposed by three needy children bodes well.  Ms. March’s evidence
with respect to the children was effusive and positive.  She has a realistic
view of their limitations and difficulties and of her role as a stepmother.  More
importantly perhaps, she is aware of the respondent’s immaturity in some areas
and is prepared to accept it.

3.7:     The Ability of Each Party to Act as a Parent

[
64
]

This issue has been discussed at length
under the previous topics.  Both the applicant and respondent are competent
parents but each has limitations.  The applicant’s hatred of the respondent and
resentment at the situation in which she finds herself limit her ability to
provide the children with the warmth and affection they need.  Her geographical
separation from her family and perhaps her personality limit her ability to
have a support system in place to assist her with the challenges of parenthood.

[
65
]

The respondent has much to learn about the
day-to-day responsibilities of being a parent.  However, he has been learning
fast and shows every indication of a willingness to continue to do so.  He is
also fortunate in having a partner whose organizational skills and willingness
to use them make up for his deficiencies in these areas.  He is also fortunate
that his parents are willing and able to provide extensive support to him with
the care of the children.

[
66
]

The sad but inescapable conclusion is that
the applicant, on her own, cannot provide the quality of parenting that the
respondent aided by Ms. March and his parents is able to provide.

3.8:     The Relationship by Blood or Adoption between Each
Party and the Child

[
67
]

This factor is neutral in this case.

4:     CONCLUSION

[
68
]

The applicant’s position is that she should
have sole custody of the children.  The respondent also believes that he should
have sole custody.  The Office of the Children’s Lawyer supports the
respondent’s position.  It is most unfortunate that no one seems able to support
the concept of shared parenting since that is, in effect, what has been going
on since the interim order in 2005.

[
69
]

The difficulty here is the animosity between
the parties particularly on the part of the applicant.  Her feelings are such
that I can have no confidence that she would not continue to attempt to
undermine a shared parenting arrangement by attacking the respondent both in
the minds of the children and by any other means at her disposal.  Shared
custody cannot be successful under such circumstances.

[
70
]

As a review of the findings set out above
will indicate, it is the home of the respondent that provides the more stable
environment for the children.  This is particularly important for David who has
high needs in terms of stability and assistance.  However, it is equally
important for Sarah and Daniel who both exhibit pronounced degrees of
insecurity in their mother’s home.  The children should have their primary
residence and home of the respondent.  In particular, weeknights should be
spent there to ensure that homework is done.

[
71
]

The children must, however, continue to see
as much of their mother as is compatible with this need.  That can be achieved
by an arrangement ensuring that they spend every second weekend from Friday
evening until Monday morning in their mother’s home and that she have them one
evening per week from after school until 8 p.m.  The winter school vacation,
the March break, and Jewish high holidays should be alternated and the children
should have four weeks during the summer school vacation with their mother.

[
72
]

The respondent should be responsible for all
decisions respecting school and the medical and dental care of the children.

ORDER

1.

The parties shall have joint
custody of the children with daily care and control exercised by the
respondent.

2.

The respondent shall have the
responsibility for determining the educational institutions to be attended by
the children, provided that no child shall change schools before the end of
the 2006-2007 school year.

3.

The children shall have access
with the applicant as follows:

(a)

every second weekend from Friday
after school until Monday morning at the beginning of school, or Tuesday
morning if Monday is a holiday,

(b)

each Wednesday from after school
until 8:00 p.m.,

(c)

alternate December school
holidays, March school holidays, and Jewish High holidays.

(d)

four weeks during the summer school
vacation,

(e)

such other times for special
events or occasions as the parties may agree upon from time to time.
